prompt: A table has a column `email` that is unique and never null, and a column `id` that is the primary key. What is `email` called?
hint: The word is about the possibility, not about which one was chosen.

choices.text: A candidate key
choices.why: Any column set that could have been the primary key is a candidate key; one of them was chosen.

choices.text: A foreign key
choices.why: A foreign key points at another table's key. Nothing here points anywhere.

choices.text: A surrogate key
choices.why: That is `id`: a value with no meaning outside the database, invented to be the key.

choices.text: A partial key
choices.why: There is no such thing in the relational model.

prompt: Why does `NULL = NULL` evaluate to unknown rather than to true?
hint: Think about what the value is standing in for.

choices.text: Because the comparison is deferred to the index
choices.why: Nothing about this involves an index.

choices.text: A null is an absence, not a value
choices.why: Two unknown ages are not an assertion that the ages match, so the comparison has nothing to stand on.

choices.text: Because the standard reserves the case
choices.why: It falls out of three-valued logic rather than being a special case.

choices.text: Because SQL compares nulls by identity
choices.why: There is no identity to compare; there is no value.

prompt: An `orders.customer_id` foreign key is declared `ON DELETE RESTRICT`. A customer with three orders is deleted. What happens?
hint: Two of these describe a different clause.

choices.text: The orders are deleted with the customer
choices.why: That is CASCADE.

choices.text: The `customer_id` on the three orders becomes null
choices.why: That is SET NULL.

choices.text: The orders are kept and point at a customer that is gone
choices.why: That is precisely the state a foreign key exists to prevent.

choices.text: The delete is refused
choices.why: RESTRICT refuses while a child row still points at the parent.

prompt: A junction table records which students are enrolled on which courses, one row per enrolment. What should its primary key be?
hint: What makes one row of this table different from another?

choices.text: `student_id` alone
choices.why: A student takes more than one course.

choices.text: An added `id` column
choices.why: It permits the same pair twice, which is the one thing this table must not allow.

choices.text: The pair `(student_id, course_id)`
choices.why: The pair is what a row asserts, so the pair is the identity.

choices.text: `course_id` alone
choices.why: A course has more than one student.

prompt: In the relational model the formal word for a table is a ___, and the formal word for one of its rows is a ___.
hint: One names the set; the other names a member of it.

prompt: You are told a natural key — the citizen's tax number — is better than a surrogate `id` because it carries meaning. What is the strongest argument against it?
hint: Think about what happens after the row is written.

choices.text: It is refused as a unique constraint on a large table
choices.why: It is accepted as one.

choices.text: Every row pointing at it moves too
choices.why: A tax number entered wrongly is corrected sometimes, and a key that carries meaning inherits every correction that meaning needs.

choices.text: It is slower to index, and the index can be large
choices.why: Marginal, and not the reason.

choices.text: It is longer to type, so it tends to be mistyped
choices.why: True and trivial.

prompt: What does it mean to say a relational table has no inherent order?
hint: What has to be written for an order to exist?

choices.text: An ORDER BY is applied to every query automatically
choices.why: It is not.

choices.text: Rows come back in the order they were inserted, unless a page was reused
choices.why: That is common and never promised, which is worse than it being false.

choices.text: Without ORDER BY, no order is promised
choices.why: Any order you observe is an accident of the plan and may change with the data or the version.

choices.text: Rows are stored alphabetically until an index says otherwise
choices.why: Nothing stores them alphabetically.

prompt: A table of orders stores `customer_id`, `customer_name` and `customer_city`. Which normal form does this break, and why?
hint: The customer's name depends on which customer, not on which order.

choices.text: First, because a column holds more than one value
choices.why: Each of these holds one value.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: The repetition here is exactly what third normal form is about.

choices.text: Second, because part of a composite key determines a column
choices.why: That needs a composite key, and this table has a single-column one.

choices.text: Third: a non-key column determines another
choices.why: `customer_id` determines the name and the city, and it is not the key of this table.

prompt: A `phones` column holds the string `'11 9999-0000, 11 8888-1111'`. Which normal form is broken?
hint: Count the values in one cell.

choices.text: The first
choices.why: A cell holds one value, and this holds two.

choices.text: The second
choices.why: That is about partial dependency on a composite key.

choices.text: Boyce-Codd
choices.why: That is a stricter version of the third, about overlapping candidate keys.

choices.text: The third
choices.why: That is about a non-key column determining another.

prompt: An invoice line stores the product's price at the time of sale, and the product table also has a price. A reviewer calls this a third normal form violation. Are they right?
hint: Ask whether the two numbers are the same fact.

choices.text: No — the third normal form applies to keys rather than to values
choices.why: It applies to every non-key column.

choices.text: Yes — any repeated column breaks the third normal form
choices.why: Normal forms are about dependency, not about a column name appearing twice.

choices.text: Yes — the price is derivable from the product
choices.why: Today's price is. The price on a sale from last March is not.

choices.text: No — the two are different facts
choices.why: The price on the line is what was charged; the price on the product is what it costs today. One is history and cannot be recomputed from the other.

prompt: What does a deliberate denormalisation cost that a normalised design does not?
hint: Think about what happens on a write.

choices.text: Every write has to update the copy too
choices.why: A missed one is a lie nothing reports: the duplicate is yours to keep true, on every path that writes, forever.

choices.text: A slower read on the duplicated column
choices.why: The read is what it buys, not what it costs.

choices.text: More disk, and the backup time that comes with it
choices.why: Disk is the cheap half.

choices.text: The loss of foreign keys on the table
choices.why: Nothing about a copy removes a constraint.

prompt: Put these four states of one table in order, from least normalised to most.
items: A `tags` column holding a comma-separated list
One row per tag, with the article's title repeated on each
One row per tag, with the article's id and its title
A `tags` table and a junction table, with no title copied
trap: The middle two look interchangeable: both have one row per tag, and the difference is whether what is repeated is the key or the words.

prompt: A reporting query joins seven tables and takes four seconds. Which is the honest first question before denormalising?
hint: One of these is free to answer and the rest are work.

choices.text: Whether to move to a wider machine
choices.why: Hardware buys a constant factor and hides the reason.

choices.text: Whether the indexes the plan wants are there
choices.why: Most seven-table joins are slow because one of them is a sequential scan, and reading the plan says which.

choices.text: Whether to cache the result for five minutes
choices.why: That makes the report stale rather than fast.

choices.text: Whether to add a summary table
choices.why: That is a decision to take after you know why it is slow.

prompt: Why should money be stored as `numeric` rather than as `float`?
hint: Ask what the type promises about arithmetic.

choices.text: A float is slower to add
choices.why: It is faster, which is the temptation.

choices.text: A float is refused in a CHECK constraint on a money column
choices.why: It is accepted.

choices.text: A float has no exact 0.10, so sums drift
choices.why: Binary floating point cannot represent a tenth, and the error accumulates across a ledger until a total is visibly wrong.

choices.text: A float is limited to six digits
choices.why: A double carries about fifteen.

prompt: A column is `timestamp without time zone` and the application writes local times from two countries. What has been lost?
hint: Two readings of one number.

choices.text: The ability to sort the column
choices.why: It sorts. It sorts wrongly, which is the problem.

choices.text: The ability to index the column
choices.why: It indexes.

choices.text: Which instant each row is about
choices.why: Without the offset, 09:00 in São Paulo and 09:00 in Lisbon are the same stored number and different moments.

choices.text: The precision below the second
choices.why: Precision is a separate property and is still there.

prompt: Match each ALTER TABLE to the work it does on a large table.
hint: One only writes a line in the catalogue.

pairs.right: Catalogue only

pairs.left: ADD COLUMN with a volatile default
pairs.right: Rewrites every row
Reads every row and writes none
Marks it dead and reclaims the space later

right_distractors: Runs without any lock at all
Is refused while the table has rows

prompt: A constraint added as NOT VALID skips the check on the rows that are already there. To check them afterwards without blocking writes you run ALTER TABLE … ___ CONSTRAINT.
hint: One word, and it is not `CHECK`.

prompt: What is the difference between `varchar(50)` and `text` in PostgreSQL?
hint: One of them refuses something.

choices.text: `text` cannot be indexed without an operator class
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: `varchar` is stored inline and `text` out of line
choices.why: Both follow the same rule, decided by size rather than by type.

choices.text: `varchar` is faster for short strings
choices.why: It is not measurably faster.

choices.text: The length limit, and nothing else
choices.why: They share one storage format; the limit is a constraint expressed inside the type rather than a different way of keeping the bytes.

prompt: A CHECK constraint and application-level validation both express one rule. Why keep the CHECK?
hint: Count the ways a row can arrive.

choices.text: Other writers reach the table too
choices.why: A migration, a script and a second service each write here, and the constraint is the only rule all of them meet.

choices.text: The CHECK is faster than the application's test
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: The CHECK gives a better error message
choices.why: It usually gives a worse one.

choices.text: The CHECK lets the planner skip rows it knows cannot match
choices.why: A CHECK can inform the planner, and that is a side effect rather than the reason.

prompt: `WHERE status <> 'shipped'` returns fewer rows than expected. What is the most likely reason?
hint: Something in the column is neither equal nor unequal.

choices.text: A case difference in the stored values
choices.why: That would be a reason, and it would change which rows match rather than silently dropping a class of them.

choices.text: Rows where `status` is null
choices.why: A null compares to nothing, so `<>` is unknown and the row is dropped.

choices.text: A missing index on `status`
choices.why: An index changes speed and never the result.

choices.text: A trailing space in the literal
choices.why: Possible, and it would not single out a whole group of rows.

prompt: A page of results uses `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`. Two rows share the same `created_at`. What can go wrong?
hint: What decides the order between the two of them?

choices.text: A row appears twice, or not at all
choices.why: The tie is broken by the plan, which may differ between the two queries that fetch the two pages.

choices.text: The query is refused as ambiguous by the planner
choices.why: It runs.

choices.text: The second page is always empty
choices.why: It is not.

choices.text: The rows come back in insertion order
choices.why: Nothing promises that.

prompt: Which of these WHERE clauses lets an index on `created_at` be used?
hint: One side of the comparison has to be the bare column.

choices.text: `WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-03-01'`
choices.why: The function wraps the column, so the index on the raw value no longer matches.

choices.text: `WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-02'`
choices.why: The column stands alone, so the index range applies.

choices.text: `WHERE extract(year from created_at) = 2026`
choices.why: Same problem: the column is inside a function.

choices.text: `WHERE created_at + interval '1 day' > now()`
choices.why: The arithmetic is on the column rather than on the constant.

prompt: To bring back rows whose `name` starts with the letters `an` and ignores what follows, you write WHERE name LIKE ___ — and the wildcard for a single character is ___.
hint: Two symbols, and one of them is a single character.

prompt: What does `SELECT DISTINCT a, b` do?
hint: Read it as one thing rather than two.

choices.text: Removes repeated values of `a` only
choices.why: That would need a different construct.

choices.text: Removes repeats in each column separately
choices.why: That would produce columns of different lengths, which is not a table.

choices.text: Sorts the result and removes neighbouring repeats
choices.why: A sort is one way to implement it and is not promised.

choices.text: Removes repeated pairs of `a` and `b`
choices.why: DISTINCT applies to the whole row the select produces, not to one column.

prompt: `ORDER BY name` puts `Ana` before `ana` on one server and after it on another. What explains it?
hint: Something about the database decides what order letters are in.

choices.text: The client's locale
choices.why: The sort happens on the server.

choices.text: Whether an index exists on `name`
choices.why: An index follows the collation rather than deciding it.

choices.text: The collation it was created with
choices.why: Ordering text is a property of the collation, and two servers can be set up with different ones.

choices.text: The version of the SQL standard each one follows
choices.why: The standard leaves this to the collation.

prompt: A LEFT JOIN is written with the filter on the right table in the WHERE clause instead of in the ON clause. What does that do?
hint: Ask when each of the two is applied.

choices.text: It is refused by the parser as ambiguous
choices.why: It runs without a word of complaint.

choices.text: It leaves the result the same on both sides
choices.why: That is true of an inner join and false here.

choices.text: It turns the join into an inner join
choices.why: The unmatched rows come back with nulls and the WHERE then drops them, which is what an inner join does.

choices.text: It makes the join faster on a large table
choices.why: It changes the result, which is worse than changing the speed.

prompt: Table A has 3 rows, table B has 4, and each A row matches exactly 2 B rows. How many rows does an inner join produce?
hint: Count per row of A.

choices.why: That adds the two counts instead of multiplying the matches.
That is the size of B.
That is the cross join, which is every pair.
Three rows of A, two matches each.

prompt: A report joins `orders` to `order_items` and sums `orders.total`. The totals come out far too high. What happened?

choices.text: Some orders have a null total

choices.why: The join repeats the order row for every item, and the sum adds each copy.

choices.text: The totals are stored in cents

pairs.right: Neither side's
The left table's
The right table's

Only the first match of each

prompt: You want customers who have never placed an order. Which of these gets it wrong?
hint: One of them behaves differently when a null turns up in the subquery.

choices.text: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`
choices.why: One null `customer_id` makes NOT IN return no rows at all, silently.

choices.text: A LEFT JOIN with `WHERE o.id IS NULL`
choices.why: The anti-join written by hand, and it is correct.

choices.text: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id)`
choices.why: EXISTS is about whether a row is there, so a null is simply a row that does not match.

choices.text: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL)`
choices.why: The null is excluded, so NOT IN behaves.

prompt: A join of a table with itself needs each side to be given a different name. The keyword for that name is ___, and the join that produces every possible pair is called a ___ join.
hint: The second one is two words in some dialects and one here.

prompt: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
hint: One of them can see the aggregate.

choices.text: HAVING is the older spelling of WHERE
choices.why: They are different clauses at different stages.

choices.text: HAVING filters rows, WHERE filters groups
choices.why: The two are the other way round.

choices.text: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
choices.why: WHERE runs before the grouping, so it cannot see a count; HAVING runs after.

choices.text: WHERE is refused when GROUP BY is present
choices.why: It is accepted, and it is usually what you want.

prompt: A column holds 10 rows, three of them null. What do `count(*)` and `count(column)` return?
hint: One of them counts rows and the other counts values.

choices.text: 10 and 10
choices.why: That would make the two spellings the same.

choices.text: 7 and 10
choices.why: The two are the other way round.

choices.text: 7 and 7
choices.why: The star is not affected by a null in any column.

choices.text: 10 and 7
choices.why: The star counts rows; the column counts the values that are there.

prompt: What does a window function do that GROUP BY does not?
hint: Count the rows that come back.

choices.text: It can be used inside a WHERE clause
choices.why: It cannot: the window is computed after the WHERE.

choices.text: It keeps every row
choices.why: A group collapses its rows into one; a window leaves them and computes the aggregate over a frame beside each.

choices.text: It computes faster over a large table
choices.why: Speed is not the distinction and often goes the other way.

choices.text: It works without an ORDER BY in the query
choices.why: So does a GROUP BY.

prompt: Match each ranking function to how it numbers a tie of two rows followed by a third.
hint: Two of them agree on the tie and disagree on what comes next.

prompt: `SELECT department, name, count(*) FROM staff GROUP BY department` is refused. Why?
hint: One column is neither grouped nor aggregated.

choices.text: `name` is neither grouped nor aggregated
choices.why: The group holds many names and the query does not say which one to show.

choices.text: A GROUP BY needs at least two columns to be valid
choices.why: One is fine.

choices.text: `department` has to be repeated in an ORDER BY
choices.why: Ordering is a separate matter.

choices.text: `count(*)` needs an alias before it can be selected
choices.why: An alias is a convenience.

prompt: A table of 1000 sales has 4 regions. A query groups by region and takes the average. How many rows does it return?
hint: One per group.

prompt: What distinguishes a correlated subquery from an uncorrelated one?
hint: Ask how many times it has to be evaluated.

choices.text: It appears in the FROM clause
choices.why: That is a derived table and is a separate thing.

choices.text: It returns more than one column
choices.why: Either kind can.

choices.text: It refers to a column of the outer query
choices.why: That reference is what ties it to each outer row, so it is evaluated per row.

choices.text: It is written with the EXISTS keyword
choices.why: EXISTS is common there and is not the definition.

prompt: A view is described as 'a stored query, not stored data'. What follows from that?
hint: Ask what happens when the underlying table changes.

choices.text: Reading it runs the query again
choices.why: So it is always current and never faster: there is nothing stored to go stale and nothing stored to read quickly.

choices.text: It cannot be used inside another query or another view
choices.why: It is used exactly like a table.

choices.text: It has to be refreshed after a write
choices.why: That is a materialised view.

choices.text: Reading it is faster because the plan is kept
choices.why: That is closer to a materialised view, and even there the plan is not the point.

prompt: A recursive CTE is written to walk a tree of categories and never finishes. What is the most likely cause?
hint: Something about the data rather than about the SQL.

choices.text: The UNION ALL should have been UNION
choices.why: UNION would mask a cycle by removing duplicates, which is a patch rather than the cause.

choices.text: A cycle in the parent references
choices.why: A category that is its own ancestor makes the recursion produce rows for ever.

choices.text: A missing index on the parent column
choices.why: That makes it slow and not endless.

choices.text: The base case selects too many rows
choices.why: A large base case finishes.

prompt: When is a materialised view the right answer rather than a plain view?
hint: Two conditions have to hold together.

choices.text: The underlying tables are small and rarely written
choices.why: Then the plain view is already fast.

choices.text: The data is allowed to be old, whatever the query costs
choices.why: A cheap query gains nothing and adds a refresh to maintain.

choices.text: The query is expensive, whatever the freshness requirement
choices.why: Serving stale numbers to somebody who needs current ones is worse than being slow.

choices.text: The query is expensive and the data is allowed to be a little old
choices.why: Both halves are needed: the cost is what it buys back, and the staleness is what it costs.

prompt: Match each letter of ACID to what it promises.
hint: One is about other transactions and one is about the power going out.

pairs.right: All of it happens, or none of it
The rules hold before and after
Concurrent work does not leak in
A commit survives a crash

prompt: Two transactions each read a balance of 100 and each write 100 minus their own withdrawal. One withdrawal is lost. Which anomaly is this?
hint: Both read before either wrote.

choices.text: A lost update
choices.why: The second write is computed from a value the first write already replaced.

choices.text: A non-repeatable read
choices.why: Close, and that names re-reading a row rather than losing a write.

choices.text: A dirty read
choices.why: Neither read anything uncommitted.

choices.text: A phantom read
choices.why: That is about rows appearing in a repeated range query.

prompt: What does READ COMMITTED promise that READ UNCOMMITTED does not?
hint: One word about what you are allowed to see.

choices.text: A row you read twice gives the same answer
choices.why: That is REPEATABLE READ.

choices.text: You never see another transaction's uncommitted writes
choices.why: That is the dirty read, and it is the one anomaly this level removes.

choices.text: Your writes are never blocked by a reader
choices.why: That is a property of the concurrency mechanism rather than of the level.

choices.text: A range query returns the same rows twice
choices.why: That is about phantoms, one level further up.

prompt: Two transactions update the same two rows in opposite order and both stop. What does the database do?
hint: Waiting for ever is not one of the options it takes.

choices.text: It merges the two updates in commit order
choices.why: There is nothing to merge; neither can proceed.

choices.text: It refuses the second transaction at its first statement
choices.why: The first statement of each succeeds; the cycle closes at the second.

choices.text: It detects the cycle and aborts one of them
choices.why: A deadlock is a cycle in the wait graph, and the only way out is to end one side.

choices.text: It waits until one of them times out on the client
choices.why: That would make a deadlock look like a hang.

prompt: What is the simplest discipline that makes deadlocks rare in application code?
hint: It is about the order, not about the level.

choices.text: Keep transactions open longer so they finish together
choices.why: Longer transactions collide more.

choices.text: Retry the whole transaction on any error
choices.why: Retrying is the fallback after the discipline, and on its own it hides the cause.

choices.text: Raise the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: That produces more aborts rather than fewer.

choices.text: Take locks on rows in a consistent order everywhere
choices.why: A cycle needs two paths taking the same locks in opposite orders; one order removes the cycle.

prompt: A long-running transaction is left open by mistake on a busy table. What is the cost?
hint: Think about what the database cannot throw away.

choices.text: Old row versions cannot be cleaned up
choices.why: Cleanup cannot pass the oldest open snapshot, so the table and its indexes grow for as long as it is left open.

choices.text: Queries on other tables begin to fail
choices.why: They carry on.

choices.text: The write-ahead log stops being written
choices.why: It keeps being written, which is part of the pressure.

choices.text: Indexes on the table are dropped automatically
choices.why: Nothing drops an index on its own.

prompt: Put the four isolation levels in order, from the one that permits most anomalies to the one that permits fewest.
trap: The two in the middle are the ones people swap: committed data can still change between two reads, and that is what the third level closes.

prompt: An index exists on `(country, city)`. Which query cannot use it?
hint: The leftmost prefix rule.

choices.text: `WHERE country = 'BR'`
choices.why: The first column alone is a leftmost prefix.

choices.text: `WHERE city = 'Recife' AND country = 'BR'`
choices.why: The order in the WHERE does not matter; the planner reads it as a set.

choices.text: `WHERE city = 'Recife'`
choices.why: City is sorted only within each country, so on its own it is scattered through the index.

choices.text: `WHERE country = 'BR' AND city = 'Recife'`
choices.why: Both columns, in the index's order.

prompt: What makes an index 'covering' for a particular query?
hint: Ask whether the table has to be opened at all.

choices.text: The index is larger than the table
choices.why: Size is a consequence rather than a definition.

choices.text: The index is the primary key's
choices.why: A primary key index covers a query only if it happens to hold the columns.

choices.text: The index is declared UNIQUE
choices.why: Uniqueness is a constraint and says nothing about which columns are read.

choices.text: The index holds every column the query reads
choices.why: Then the answer is assembled from the index and the table is never visited.

prompt: Why does an extra index make writes slower?
hint: Count what has to be kept in step.

choices.text: The table is locked while the index is read
choices.why: Reading an index does not lock the table.

choices.text: Every insert and update has to maintain it too
choices.why: An index is a second ordered copy, and it is kept in step inside the same transaction.

choices.text: The planner has more options to consider
choices.why: Planning cost is real and tiny beside the write.

choices.text: The write-ahead log is disabled for indexed tables
choices.why: It is not disabled anywhere.

prompt: A query filters on a boolean column where 95% of rows are true. Why might the planner ignore an index on it?
hint: Compare the cost of the two ways of reading almost everything.

choices.text: Most of the table is cheaper to scan
choices.why: Each index hit is a jump to a page; at ninety-five per cent the jumps cost more than reading the pages in order.

choices.text: Boolean columns are not indexable on their own
choices.why: They are.

choices.text: The index is too small for the planner to consider
choices.why: Size is not the objection.

choices.text: The planner ignores indexes on columns with two values
choices.why: It weighs the cost rather than applying a rule about the type.

prompt: What does a partial index give you that a full one does not?
hint: It is defined with a WHERE.

choices.text: It allows duplicate values where a full index would not
choices.why: Uniqueness is a separate declaration.

choices.text: It updates itself less often than a full index
choices.why: It updates whenever an indexed row changes.

choices.text: It can be used by queries that do not mention its condition
choices.why: The planner has to prove the query implies the condition.

choices.text: It indexes only the rows you care about, so it is smaller
choices.why: A predicate on the index keeps out the rows no query asks for, which is most of them in a status column.

prompt: Creating an index normally blocks writes for as long as it takes. The PostgreSQL option that builds it without that block is CREATE INDEX ___, and it pays for that by scanning the table ___ times.
hint: The number is small and is not one.

prompt: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
hint: One of them runs the query.

choices.text: ANALYZE updates the table statistics first
choices.why: That is the separate ANALYZE command, and the collision of names is the trap.

choices.text: ANALYZE shows the plan in more detail without running it
choices.why: It runs it, which matters on an UPDATE.

choices.text: ANALYZE executes it and reports what actually happened
choices.why: The plain form shows the plan and the estimates; ANALYZE adds the real rows and the real time.

choices.text: ANALYZE forces the planner to pick the cheapest plan
choices.why: The planner already tries to.

prompt: A plan estimates 12 rows and the actual count is 480,000. What does that most often mean?
hint: The planner chose its method using the estimate.

choices.text: The table is missing a primary key
choices.why: Estimates do not depend on there being one.

choices.text: The statistics no longer describe the data
choices.why: They are stale, or the predicate is one they cannot express — and a wrong estimate makes the planner pick a nested loop for a huge set.

choices.text: The row count is reported in kilobytes rather than in rows
choices.why: It is a count of rows.

choices.text: The query has a syntax error the planner tolerated
choices.why: A syntax error never runs.

prompt: Match each join method to the shape of input it suits.
hint: One of them wants both sides already in order.

pairs.right: A small outer side and an index on the inner
One side small enough to hold in memory
Both sides sorted on the join key

right_distractors: A table with no statistics collected

prompt: A sequential scan appears in a plan. When is that the right thing to see?
hint: Ask what fraction of the table the query wants.

choices.text: When the query reads a large share of the table
choices.why: Reading pages in order beats jumping to most of them through an index.

choices.text: When the table has an index on the filtered column
choices.why: Then the question is which is cheaper, and the index usually wins for a small share.

choices.text: When the query has an ORDER BY
choices.why: An ordering may favour an index rather than a scan.

choices.text: When the table was written to recently
choices.why: Recency is not part of the choice.

prompt: In a plan, what does a node's `loops` count tell you?
hint: It multiplies something else on the same line.

choices.text: How many rows it returned in total
choices.why: That is the rows figure, and it is also per loop.

choices.text: How many times the planner reconsidered the node
choices.why: Planning happens once, before execution.

choices.text: How many workers were used in parallel
choices.why: Workers are reported separately.

choices.text: How many times the node ran
choices.why: Its time and its rows are per loop, so a node showing 0.1 ms with 40,000 loops took four seconds and the line looks fast.

prompt: What is the N+1 problem?
hint: Count the round trips, not the rows.

choices.text: One query returning N times too many rows
choices.why: That is a join fan-out, which is a different mistake.

choices.text: N queries running at once and exhausting the pool
choices.why: That is pool exhaustion.

choices.text: One query for the list, then one per item
choices.why: The loop over the list issues a query each time, so a page of fifty costs fifty-one.

choices.text: A query retried N times after a deadlock
choices.why: That is a retry storm.

prompt: Which fixes an N+1 without changing what the code reads?
hint: The word is about when the related rows are fetched.

choices.text: Raising the connection pool size
choices.why: That serves the same problem with more connections.

choices.text: Eager loading the association in one extra query
choices.why: The related rows are fetched once for the whole list rather than per item.

choices.text: Caching each row after the first read
choices.why: That helps on the second page and not on the first.

choices.text: Adding an index on the foreign key
choices.why: That makes each of the fifty queries faster and leaves fifty of them.

prompt: Why should a migration be written so that the old code still works after it runs?
hint: Think about the minutes during a deploy.

choices.text: Both versions are live while the deploy rolls
choices.why: The migration lands before every instance has been replaced, so the old code meets the new schema.

choices.text: It makes the rollback script shorter
choices.why: A rollback is a consequence rather than the reason.

choices.text: It lets the migration run inside a transaction
choices.why: That depends on the statements rather than on compatibility.

choices.text: It avoids locking the table during the change
choices.why: Locking is a separate concern with its own techniques.

prompt: Put the four deploys of an online column rename in order.
items: Add the new column and write to both
Backfill the old rows into the new column
Move every read to the new column
Stop writing the old column and drop it
trap: Moving the reads before the backfill is the swap that looks harmless: the new column is being written, so it looks populated, and every row older than the deploy comes back empty.

prompt: An ORM is described as a leaky abstraction. What does that mean in practice here?
hint: Ask what you still have to know.

choices.text: It cannot express a join
choices.why: Every ORM can.

choices.text: It requires a specific database
choices.why: Most support several.

choices.text: You still have to know what SQL it emits
choices.why: The abstraction saves the typing and not the understanding; the plan is still yours to read.

choices.text: It loses rows under concurrency
choices.why: That would be a defect rather than a leak.

prompt: Why is a migration that both changes the schema and backfills data in one statement a bad shape on a large table?
hint: Think about how long one lock is held.

choices.text: It cannot be rolled back at all
choices.why: In a transactional DDL database it can.

choices.text: It holds a lock for the whole backfill
choices.why: Schema changes take a strong lock, and a backfill of millions of rows keeps it for minutes.

choices.text: It is refused when the table has an index
choices.why: It is accepted.

choices.text: The backfill runs before the schema change
choices.why: Statements run in the order written.

prompt: Which of these is the strongest reason to choose SQLite for an application?
hint: Think about where the database runs.

choices.text: It replicates across machines out of the box
choices.why: That needs something on top.

choices.text: It handles many concurrent writers well
choices.why: That is the one thing it is not for.

choices.text: It has the richest set of index types available
choices.why: PostgreSQL has more.

choices.text: The data lives beside the program
choices.why: It is a library in the process rather than a server, and its writing is serialised — one writer is the shape it is built for.

prompt: MySQL and MariaDB share a history. What is the honest summary of the difference today?
hint: One of them is governed differently from the other.

choices.text: One supports transactions and the other does not
choices.why: Both do, through InnoDB and its descendants.

choices.text: A fork that has drifted apart
choices.why: They began identical and have diverged in features and in who decides them, so a feature is no longer assumed to exist in both.

choices.text: The same code released under two different names
choices.why: They were, and are no longer.

choices.text: One is a column store and the other a row store
choices.why: Both store rows by default.

prompt: A team picks a database because it is what they know. When is that the right call?
hint: Compare the cost of learning against the cost of the mismatch.

choices.text: Only for a prototype that will be thrown away
choices.why: Prototypes are kept, and the argument is better than this.

choices.text: Never — the workload decides on its own
choices.why: Operating a database you do not know is a cost nobody counts until the first incident.

choices.text: Whenever the team is under a deadline
choices.why: A deadline makes the wrong engine more expensive rather than less.

choices.text: When the workload asks for nothing else
choices.why: Familiarity is a real advantage, and it stops paying the moment a requirement needs what the other engine offers.

prompt: Match each engine to the property most often given as its reason.
hint: Two of these are servers and one is not.

pairs.right: Breadth of types, indexes and extensions
Ubiquity in shared hosting and old stacks
No server at all, a file beside the program

right_distractors: A licence that forbids commercial use

prompt: Oracle licensing is usually counted per processor. What makes the number hard to predict?
hint: The count is not the number of chips.

choices.text: Cores are multiplied by a published factor
choices.why: The factor depends on the chip, so two machines that look identical need different counts.

choices.text: The price changes with the number of users
choices.why: That is the other metric, and it is chosen instead of this one.

choices.text: It is counted per database rather than per machine
choices.why: The processor metric is about the hardware.

choices.text: Virtual machines are always excluded from the count
choices.why: Virtualisation makes the count harder rather than removing it.

prompt: PL/SQL code is often described as the thing that keeps a company on Oracle. Why?
hint: Ask where the business rules ended up.

choices.text: It runs faster than any application language
choices.why: Speed is not what holds the company.

choices.text: The code is encrypted on disk and cannot be read back
choices.why: It can be read, and wrapping is optional and rare.

choices.text: The business logic lives in the database
choices.why: Years of it, with no equivalent elsewhere: moving the data is a week and moving the procedures is a rewrite nobody budgeted.

choices.text: The licence forbids porting it
choices.why: The obstacle is the work rather than the terms.

prompt: Oracle's default isolation behaves differently from PostgreSQL's in one respect worth knowing before a migration. Which?
hint: One of them never makes a reader wait.

choices.text: Readers are served from an undo image
choices.why: Both engines avoid blocking readers; Oracle rebuilds the older image from undo where PostgreSQL keeps row versions in the table.

choices.text: Oracle commits every statement on its own
choices.why: That is a client setting elsewhere, and Oracle's default is an explicit commit.

choices.text: Oracle has no concept of a transaction at all
choices.why: It has.

choices.text: Oracle takes a table lock on every UPDATE
choices.why: It locks rows.

prompt: A server has one socket of 24 physical cores, with a core factor of 0.5. How many processor licences does it need?
hint: Cores times the factor, rounded up.

prompt: What does a UNIQUE constraint allow that a PRIMARY KEY does not?
hint: One value is treated specially by one of them.

choices.text: A column of a type that cannot be compared
choices.why: Both need a comparable type.

choices.text: More than one column in the declaration
choices.why: Both can be declared over several columns.

choices.text: A null, and in most engines more than one
choices.why: A primary key refuses nulls; unique treats each null as distinct from every other.

choices.text: Two rows carrying the very same value
choices.why: That is what both of them refuse.

prompt: Why is `SELECT *` discouraged in application code?
hint: Think about what happens when somebody adds a column.

choices.text: It prevents the use of any index
choices.why: Indexes are chosen from the WHERE and the ORDER BY.

choices.text: It is slower to parse than a column list
choices.why: Parsing is not where the cost is.

choices.text: It is refused by most database drivers
choices.why: Every driver accepts it.

choices.text: The set of columns changes under the code
choices.why: A column added tomorrow arrives unannounced, and one removed breaks a read nothing warned about.

prompt: An UPDATE with no WHERE is run by mistake on a production table inside an open transaction. What is the correct next action?
hint: The transaction has not ended yet.

choices.text: Run the reverse UPDATE from memory
choices.why: The old values are gone from the session and only the rollback still has them.

choices.text: ROLLBACK, before anything else
choices.why: Nothing is durable until the commit, so the whole statement can still be undone.

choices.text: COMMIT and then restore from the backup
choices.why: That makes the mistake permanent and then undoes it expensively.

choices.text: Close the client and let the server decide
choices.why: It rolls back, and doing it by accident is not a procedure.

prompt: Which is the honest description of what an index is?
hint: It is not a copy of the table.

choices.text: A compressed copy of the whole table
choices.why: It holds the indexed columns rather than the row.

choices.text: A hint telling the planner which rows to prefer
choices.why: It is a structure that is read, not advice.

choices.text: An ordered structure over some columns, plus pointers
choices.why: The order is what allows a search to discard most of the table without reading it.

choices.text: A cache of the rows most recently read
choices.why: That is the buffer pool.

prompt: A query that groups sales by month and gives each row its group's total without collapsing the rows is written with the keyword ___, and the clause that defines which rows the calculation sees is ___ BY.
hint: The second word also appears in a different clause of the same query.

prompt: A `status` column is a free-text string and three spellings of 'cancelled' are in the table. What would have prevented it?
hint: Something that refuses a value at the moment it is written.

choices.text: A nightly job normalising the values
choices.why: That cleans up after the fact and never catches up.

choices.text: A NOT NULL on the column
choices.why: That refuses absence rather than a spelling.

choices.text: An index on the column
choices.why: An index orders values and refuses none.

choices.text: A CHECK listing the values, or a lookup table
choices.why: Either refuses the fourth spelling at the write, where the fix is cheap.

prompt: Two services write to one table and a third reads it. Where does the rule that the status may only move forwards belong?
hint: Count how many places would have to agree.

choices.text: In the database, where every writer meets it
choices.why: A rule in one service is a rule the other one does not have, and nothing reports the difference.

choices.text: In the reader, which can ignore bad rows
choices.why: By then the row is written and the history is wrong.

choices.text: In a shared library both services import
choices.why: Better, and it still depends on both importing the same version.

choices.text: In whichever service writes most often
choices.why: The other writer is the one that breaks it.

prompt: What does `LIMIT 10` without an `ORDER BY` return?
hint: Ten of which rows?

choices.text: An error, because the order is undefined
choices.why: It runs without complaint, which is the problem.

choices.text: Ten rows, and which ten is not promised
choices.why: Without an order there is nothing to be first, so the plan decides and may decide differently tomorrow.

choices.text: The ten rows inserted first
choices.why: Common, never promised, and the difference matters.

choices.text: The ten rows with the lowest primary key
choices.why: That happens when the plan uses that index, which is an accident.

prompt: Match each symptom to the mistake behind it.
hint: Two of them are about a join and they are not the same join.

pairs.left: A sum far larger than expected
pairs.right: A join multiplying the rows

pairs.left: Rows missing from a LEFT JOIN
pairs.right: A filter in WHERE instead of ON

pairs.left: An empty result from NOT IN
pairs.right: A null inside the subquery
An ORDER BY with no tiebreaker

right_distractors: A missing index on the sorted column
A transaction left open by a client

prompt: A table grows to 400 million rows and one report is slow. Which is the wrong first move?
hint: One of these is expensive and answers nothing.

choices.text: Checking whether the statistics are current
choices.why: Cheap, and a common cause.

choices.text: Looking at which indexes the report could use
choices.why: The usual answer at any size.

choices.text: Partitioning the table
choices.why: It is a large change that helps a particular access pattern, and nobody has read the plan yet.

choices.text: Reading the plan for the slow report
choices.why: Free, and it names the problem.

prompt: Put the clauses in the order the database evaluates them.
trap: SELECT is written first and evaluated late, which is why an alias defined there cannot be used in the WHERE and can be used in the ORDER BY.

prompt: Why can an alias defined in SELECT be used in ORDER BY but not in WHERE?
hint: The answer is the order of evaluation.

choices.text: WHERE runs before SELECT and ORDER BY after it
choices.why: The alias does not exist yet when the filter is applied and does exist by the time the rows are sorted.

choices.text: ORDER BY is applied on the client
choices.why: It is applied on the server.

choices.text: WHERE accepts only column names
choices.why: It accepts expressions of every kind.

choices.text: The alias is a string and not an expression
choices.why: It is a name for an expression.

prompt: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
hint: One of them can have a WHERE.

choices.text: TRUNCATE removes chosen rows; DELETE empties the table
choices.why: The two are the other way round.

choices.text: TRUNCATE also removes the table's indexes
choices.why: The indexes stay and are emptied with it.

choices.text: DELETE drops the table and recreates it
choices.why: That is DROP followed by CREATE.

choices.text: DELETE removes chosen rows; TRUNCATE empties the table
choices.why: TRUNCATE takes no condition and does its work without walking the rows.

prompt: A soft delete is implemented with a `deleted_at` column. What does every query now have to remember?
hint: The rows are still there.

choices.text: To join the audit table for the reason
choices.why: A reason is optional and separate.

choices.text: To exclude the deleted rows, every single time
choices.why: One query that forgets shows a customer something they deleted, and it reads as a bug in the wrong place.

choices.text: To read the column as a boolean
choices.why: It is a timestamp, and its absence is the live state.

choices.text: To take a lock before reading
choices.why: Nothing about a soft delete needs one.

prompt: What makes `UPSERT` — insert, or update if the row is there — safer written as one statement than as a check followed by an insert?
hint: Think about two clients arriving together.

choices.text: Another writer slips in between the two
choices.why: Between the two statements a second client inserts the row, and the first one fails or duplicates.

choices.text: One statement is parsed faster
choices.why: Parsing is not the issue.

choices.text: The single statement avoids the index
choices.why: It relies on the index to find the conflict.

choices.text: The check cannot be written in SQL
choices.why: It can, and that is the temptation.

prompt: A backup is taken every night and has never been restored. What is the honest status of that backup?
hint: What has actually been demonstrated?

choices.text: Working, since the job reports success
choices.why: The job reports that it wrote a file.

choices.text: Unknown — a backup is proved by a restore
choices.why: Until one has been restored and checked, what exists is a file nobody has read.

choices.text: Unnecessary, given a replica
choices.why: A replica copies a mistake faithfully.

choices.text: Working, since the file size is right
choices.why: A truncated dump has a plausible size.

prompt: A foreign key is declared but no index exists on the referencing column. What suffers?
hint: Think about what happens when the parent row is touched.

choices.text: The constraint stops being enforced
choices.why: It is enforced either way, and that is the cost.

choices.text: Inserting into the child is refused
choices.why: It is accepted; the parent is found by its own key.

choices.text: Deleting or updating the parent scans the child
choices.why: The database has to check that no child points at the row, and with no index that is a full scan every time.

choices.text: The parent table doubles in size
choices.why: Nothing about it changes the parent.

prompt: Two rows have to be updated together or not at all, and the application does them in two statements without a transaction. What is the failure?
hint: The window is small and it is not zero.

choices.text: The two run in an undefined order
choices.why: They run in the order written.

choices.text: Neither statement is durable until a commit
choices.why: With autocommit each one commits on its own, which is the problem rather than the safeguard.

choices.text: The second statement overwrites the first
choices.why: They touch different rows.

choices.text: A crash between the two leaves half the change
choices.why: Atomicity is what a transaction buys, and without one the half-applied state is durable.

prompt: What does `COALESCE(a, b, 0)` return?
hint: It walks the list.

choices.text: The first argument that is not null
choices.why: It stops at the first one that has a value, and the zero is the fallback.

choices.text: The sum of the arguments that are not null
choices.why: It does no arithmetic.

choices.text: Null whenever any argument is null
choices.why: That is what it exists to avoid.

choices.text: Zero whenever either `a` or `b` is null
choices.why: It falls through only when both are.

prompt: A column stores an enumeration as a small integer to save space. What is the cost that shows up later?
hint: Ask what a person reading the table sees.

choices.text: The values cannot be constrained
choices.why: A CHECK works on an integer.

choices.text: The column cannot be indexed
choices.why: An integer indexes well.

choices.text: Comparisons become slower than on text
choices.why: They are faster.

choices.text: The meaning lives outside the database
choices.why: Every reader needs the mapping, and a query written in psql answers with numbers nobody can check.

prompt: Keyset pagination is offered as a replacement for OFFSET. What does it give up?
hint: Think about what a page number lets you do.

choices.text: The use of an index on the sort key
choices.why: It depends on exactly that index.

choices.text: Jumping straight to an arbitrary page
choices.why: It reads from where the last page ended, so there is no way to ask for page forty without walking there.

choices.text: The ability to sort by more than one column
choices.why: It handles several, with the comparison written as a tuple.

choices.text: A stable order across pages
choices.why: That is what it buys rather than what it gives up.

prompt: A statement that reads rows and intends to change them can reserve them against other transactions by ending with SELECT … FOR ___. The variant that lets other readers through but no other writer is FOR NO KEY ___.
hint: The same word fills both blanks.

prompt: Why is `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` dangerous to run on an UPDATE in production?
hint: Read the word ANALYZE literally.

choices.text: It rewrites the table's statistics
choices.why: That is the separate ANALYZE command.

choices.text: It disables the planner's cost model
choices.why: The model is used exactly as usual.

choices.text: It executes the statement
choices.why: The rows are really updated, so it belongs inside a transaction that is rolled back.

choices.text: It takes an exclusive lock on the table
choices.why: It takes whatever the statement takes.

prompt: What is the practical difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
hint: One of them does extra work.

choices.text: UNION works on two queries and UNION ALL on more
choices.why: Both chain to any number.

choices.text: UNION ALL removes duplicates and UNION keeps them
choices.why: The two are the other way round.

choices.text: UNION removes duplicates and UNION ALL keeps them
choices.why: Removing them costs a sort or a hash, which is why ALL is the default choice when you know there are none.

choices.text: UNION requires the same column names
choices.why: Both require compatible types; the names come from the first query.

prompt: A denormalised `order.item_count` drifts from the real count of items. Which repair is durable rather than cosmetic?
hint: Ask what will still be true next year.

choices.text: Add an index on the column
choices.why: An index has nothing to do with the value being wrong.

choices.text: Run a script now to recompute every row
choices.why: That fixes today and leaves the cause.

choices.text: Drop the column and count on every read
choices.why: Defensible, and it undoes the decision rather than repairing it.

choices.text: Make one path own the write, and check it against the truth
choices.why: A single writer plus a periodic comparison means a drift is found rather than discovered by a customer.

prompt: A query works on the developer's machine and is slow in production. What is the most common reason?
hint: The SQL is the same in both places.

choices.text: The data is a different size and shape
choices.why: A plan chosen for a thousand rows is the wrong plan for ten million, and the query text says nothing about it.

choices.text: The network is slower to the database
choices.why: That adds a constant and does not explain a slow query.

choices.text: Production runs an older SQL dialect
choices.why: Usually the same version.

choices.text: Indexes behave differently under load
choices.why: They behave the same; the plan is what differs.
